title: Getting to know your data

cells.text: Before analysing anything, analysts get to know their data: how big it is, what the columns are, and what the numbers look like. Every lesson starts by loading the data, using the same lines as last lesson.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the games table into df.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
df.head()

cells.text: `df.shape` tells you the size of the table as **(rows, columns)**, always rows first. There are no brackets after `shape`, because it's a fact about the table, not an action.

cells.prompt: df holds 15 games, and each game has 7 details (columns). What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: To get just one of the two numbers, put its position in square brackets. Python counts from **0**, so `df.shape[0]` is the rows and `df.shape[1]` is the columns.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with a number so this prints only the number of rows (15), then press Run.
hints: Rows come first, and Python counts from 0.

cells.prompt: Your turn: print only the number of columns. You should see 7. Use df.shape with the right number in square brackets, inside print().
hints: Columns are the second number, and the second position is 1.

cells.text: `df.columns` lists the names of all the columns. Like shape, it has no brackets after it.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see every column name.

cells.text: `df.describe()` makes a summary table of the **number** columns. **count** is how many cells are filled in, **mean** is the average, **min** is the smallest and **max** is the biggest. It has brackets because it's an action: it works something out.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see the summary.
In the summary, the count for rating is 13, but there are 15 games. Why? Pick a guess, then press Run to look at the last 3 games.

cells.text: **NaN** means the cell is empty ("Not a Number"). describe() only counts cells that are filled in, so the 2 games with no rating aren't counted. Spotting missing data early is a big part of an analyst's job.
`df.info()` gives a quick report on every column: its name, how many cells are filled in (non-null), and its type, such as numbers or text.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see the report. Look at the rating row: 13 non-null.
Your turn: show the summary table for the number columns again, from memory. Remember the brackets at the end.
hints: It's the action that summarises the number columns.

recap: df.shape gives (rows, columns), with shape[0] for rows and shape[1] for columns. df.columns lists the names, df.describe() summarises the numbers, and df.info() shows what's filled in. NaN means empty.
